answer.label: Nobody has ever produced a source
answer.authorDates: Author unknown · no located instance in Einstein’s lifetime
answer.sourceLine: There is no Einstein source for this — no letter, lecture, interview or manuscript, and no date. Alice Calaprice, whose collections are the standard reference for what Einstein did and did not say, carries the common form of it in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein (2010) in the section headed ‘Probably Not by Einstein’. It reads like a compressed rewrite of something he genuinely did say to the Saturday Evening Post in 1929 — and the real line is better.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Unknown — no source has ever been produced
“Logic will get you from A to B. Imagination will take you everywhere.”

source.excerpt: Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world.
trail: Start with the reference work. Calaprice’s Einstein collections sort every widely circulating line into sourced, doubtful and false. The dominant form of this saying — ‘Logic will get you from A to B. Imagination will take you everywhere’ — appears in the 2010 Ultimate edition under ‘Probably Not by Einstein’. That is the closest thing to an official verdict a quotation can get the verdict ↗.

Then look for what anyone repeating it offers as evidence. Nobody supplies a date, an occasion, a correspondent or a page — it travels on posters, paperweights and social posts with the name alone. That pattern is the signature of an internet-era attribution rather than a lost citation.

The wording on this page is itself a variant: most instances say A to B and take you everywhere, not A to Z and get. A saying with a real source has one wording; a saying with none drifts. One honest limit on our own work: we verified the ‘Probably Not by Einstein’ listing through the published reporting rather than by inspecting the printed page ourselves, and we did not have a copy of the earlier Expanded Quotable Einstein (2000) to check, so we do not assert what that edition does or does not contain.
source.excerptNote: This is not the quotation on this page. It is what Einstein actually said about imagination, to George Sylvester Viereck for The Saturday Evening Post of 26 October 1929 — a real interview, a real date, a real page. Read the two side by side and the fake one starts to sound like what it is: an aphorism engineered for a poster.

source.rightsNote: The saying itself is anonymous and unsourced, so there is no Einstein estate interest in it — there is nothing of his in it to protect. Note the trap in the other direction: if you swap in the genuine 1929 sentence, you are then quoting Einstein’s own words, which are public domain in the UK and EU since 1 January 2026 but of unresolved status in the US, where the Hebrew University of Jerusalem asserts rights. Free to use here; attribute honestly, which means not to Einstein. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) genuinely did think imagination outranked knowledge, and said so on the record more than once — which is exactly what makes this fake so durable. It is not attached to him at random. It is attached to him because it sounds like a tidier version of a real position he held, and a tidier version is what posters, mugs and paperweights want. Alice Calaprice’s collections were compiled to hold that line, and they place this saying on the wrong side of it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: There is nothing to argue with here, which is the point: no source has ever been offered, by anyone, for any wording. What is worth noticing is why this particular fake stuck.

items.why: No letter, lecture, interview, manuscript or archive number. The people who repeat it do not cite anything, and Calaprice — who catalogues the fakes as carefully as the real lines — places the common form under ‘Probably Not by Einstein’.

items.who: At least two versions in circulation
items.why: ‘A to Z… get you everywhere’ (this page) and the more common ‘A to B… take you everywhere.’ Note that A-to-B and A-to-Z mean different things — one is a single step, the other the whole alphabet — and nobody minds, because there is no original to be faithful to.

items.who: What Einstein did say about imagination
items.why: To George Sylvester Viereck for The Saturday Evening Post, 26 October 1929: ‘Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world.’ Real interview, real date, real page — and it says something specific rather than merely uplifting.

Paperweights, posters, LinkedIn posts, classroom displays. A quotation whose entire documented existence is on things you can buy is a quotation with no provenance, and the commerce is what keeps it alive the paperweight ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No source exists, in any wording. Calaprice’s Ultimate Quotable Einstein lists the common form under ‘Probably Not by Einstein’ — and the genuine 1929 line it echoes is on the record with a date and a page the verdict ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It flatters the reader in a very specific way: it tells anyone who has ever felt out-argued by a more rigorous colleague that they were the interesting one all along. That is a comfortable thing to hear, and it costs nothing to agree with.

It is also, on inspection, not saying much. Logic gets you from A to B and imagination takes you everywhere is a sentence with no friction in it — which is exactly why the real Einstein line does more work. His version names a limit, and then says where the limit is.
context.detailsSummary: How to tell a poster quote from a sourced one
detailsBody: A sourced quotation has one stable wording. This one has at least two, differing in both halves.
A sourced quotation comes with an occasion — a letter, an interview, a lecture, a date. This one has never come with any.
A sourced Einstein quotation usually has an Einstein Archives number. This one has none.
Reference works that catalogue the fakes will list it as a fake. Calaprice does.
And the giveaway: it is smoother than the real thing. Einstein’s actual sentences tend to be slightly awkward, because they are trying to be exact rather than quotable.
context.pull: It has at least two wordings and no source. Sayings with real sources have one wording.
